newsitem.title: SPAIN: Top NATO general warns Serbs not to "miscalculate".
newsitem.headline: Top NATO general warns Serbs not to "miscalculate".

text.p: NATO's top soldier in Europe, in a clear warning to hardline Bosnian Serbs, said on Wednesday the Bosnian authorities should not underestimate the determination of the international community to make peace work.
"I urge the authorities not to miscalculate the determination of NATO and the international community to see Dayton through," General George Joulwan told reporters at a NATO summit in Madrid.

Joulwan, the alliance's outgoing Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), said the 35,000-strong NATO-led force in Bosnia would insist the former warring parties implemented the Dayton peace accords which ended the 3-1/2 year war.

But he again reiterated that it was not his force's job to apprehend some 50 indicted war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic whose hardliners are in a power struggle with Serb Republic President Biljana Plavsic.
"It is the responsibility of the parties to bring these people to justice... they do belong in the Hague," Joulwan said, referring to the U.N. International Penal Tribunal in The Hague.
He added that he had received no instructions to conduct an operation to detain such people.

The NATO force is mandated to detain war criminals it may come across in the course of its duties, but not to seek them out and arrest them. Under Dayton, that task has been left to Bosnia's new authorities.
Joulwan said his troops had not been asked by their political leaders to do more.
"If they want us to do more they will have to give us the guidance," Joulwan said.
But he added that the international community was extremely concerned by the current crisis in Republika Srpska.
"It is a very delicate situation, but I would hope there would be no miscalculation by the authorities there," he said.

NATO leaders on Tuesday voiced deep concern over an alleged anti-democratic climate and abuses of police power in the Serb entity and gave their full backing to the elected Plavsic, a former Karadzic ally.

"The democratic process is being distorted in order to block the constitutional decisions of the elected president of Republika Srpska which must be respected," they said in a statement issued during the summit on NATO enlargement.
The statement called on hardliners allied to Karadzic to resolve their differences peacefully, warning that they faced even greater isolation from the international community if not.
"We will not tolerate any recourse to force or violence, or the unauthorised deployment of military or paramilitary force," the statement warned.

Opponents of Plavsic have scoffed at international warnings they were flouting the law by refusing to accept a presidential decision to dissolve parliament, threatening the prospect of two rival governments in the Bosnian Serb Republic.
The United States and European governments say Plavsic acted in line with the constitution last week when she dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly and called new elections for September 1.
